messages.subject: analysis advice (comparing avian species richness)
parts:
I=92m conducting a study of bird species richness in mature forests and=20=

mature forests experiencing low-density residential development in New=20=

Hampshire as part of my master=92s thesis.

I have 24 total transects, each 450m long (12 forested, 12 residential). =
I=20
plan to visit each transect 3 times. I=92m recording all species of birds=
=20
heard and seen within 60m of the transect and I=92m attempting to use=20
DISTANCE not necessarily to obtain density estimates, but to assign=20
probabilities of detection between the two habitat types to determine if=20=

there is a strong detection bias between forests and forests with patches=
=20
of residential development.=20

Assuming that I stratify by habitat type, and receive two different pdfs,=
=20
does anyone have any advice on how to establish whether these two=20
detection probabilities are significantly different, i.e., how great woul=
d=20
the pdf difference have to be to make inferences based on sampling betwee=
n=20
the two sample groups problematic? Would it be meaningful to pool the dat=
a=20
and compare each habitat separately to the pooled pdfs? Any=20
thoughts/advice/suggestion would be most welcome.
Will Y

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: analysis advice (comparing avian species richness)
parts:
Will:

I think I saw you ask a similar question on the Ecolog-list last week. =20
Glad you've come to the distance sampling list to recognize the role=20
that detectability will play in your assessment.

To address your question about assessing differences in detectability=20
between habitats. It is a model selection question. Get to the library=20
to get a copy of Buckland et al. (2001) "Intro. to distance sampling,"=20
and examine the example given in section 5.8.3 on pp. 170-171, where the=20
matter of whether or not to stratify is examined by example, with a=20
demonstration of how to apply model selection tools to address whether=20
detection functions differ between habitat strata. That example=20
specifically deals with point transects, but the approach is the same=20
for your situation with lines.
